extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, public-administration researchers, and policymakers interested in administrative law, rulemaking, and presidential control
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or measuring an executive agency’s prospective ability to complete policymaking tasks (especially rulemaking) — including human, material, analytical, and process dimensions — and how that capacity conditions presidential control. Focus is on notice-and-comment rulemaking but the account is general to administrative policymaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative capacity (definition and components)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadly, administrative capacity describes an agency’s prospective ability—not its willingness—to complete tasks delegated to it by the President and Congress. Capacity embodies the expertise and experience of the workforce, the material resources available to the agency, and the processes that promote efficiency and teamwork within the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central definitional rubric used throughout the Article. It aggregates human capital, material resources, and organizational/process features as the core dimensions of capacity (cites Bednar & Lewis and related literature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity versus policy outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: One should avoid confusing capacity with policy outcomes: capacity describes an agency’s prospective ability to complete a task whereas policy outcomes are the consequence of agency implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to achieve a desired outcome may result from political interference, bureaucratic resistance, or unexpected difficulties during implementation—not just a lack of capacity. The rubric warns evaluators to separate input/capacity measures from outcome measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staffing levels and workload management
rubrics_metrics.description: As a first-order condition, agencies need enough people to manage their policymaking workload. A larger workforce allows the agency to prioritize a greater number of tasks and, therefore, complete more policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and evidence: USPS vs CDC comparisons, importance of sufficient adjudicators and staff (cites Bednar, Drolc & Keiser). Use headcount and task-load measures to assess this dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive expertise (technical/scientific knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive expertise describes the scientific or technical knowledge brought to the agency by employees’ education and past careers; policymakers use this expertise to determine which policy options may achieve a particular outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should measure professional qualifications, subject-matter experience, and access to domain-specific expertise (e.g., toxicologists for environmental rules). The text cites examples about species protections and energy-product classification to illustrate substantive knowledge needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural expertise (knowledge of process, procedure, and politicking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural expertise describes the knowledge of process, procedure, and politicking attained through experience working in public service — a 'sense of what works and what doesn’t' and 'decision-making expertise' that reconciles evidence, political demands, legal commands, and other considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes tacit knowledge of how to navigate APA rulemaking, interagency review, timing, consultation strategy, and how to marshal evidence. Procedural expertise enables effective maneuvering through complex administrative procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team production and internal processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Rarely does a single employee contribute all expertise; agency policymakers work in teams. Capacity includes processes that promote efficiency and teamwork within the agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate organizational structures, cross-disciplinary teams, project management practices, and formal/informal procedures that enable coordination (cites team-production literature and examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment-processing capacity (ability to review and respond to public comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking often generates thousands of public comments; agencies require staff, systems, and sometimes temporary facilities to review and respond to significant comments (e.g., FDA’s warehouse and temporary workers for >710,000 comments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure technological and human capacity for comment intake, review, categorization, and reasoned response. Legal thresholds matter (must respond to 'comments which are of cogent materiality'); capacity shortfalls here can produce legal vulnerability (cites Nova Scotia, Ohio v. EPA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical and procedural-compliance capacity (cost–benefit, regulatory analyses, OIRA review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policymaking requires agencies to perform numerous analytical tasks (cost–benefit analysis, small-entity analysis, environmental and economic impacts) and to satisfy OIRA and other oversight requirements before issuing final rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the agency’s in-house analytic capability, access to data and models, and capacity to conduct mandated analyses. The Article cites Exec. Order requirements, OMB Circular A‑4, statutory thresholds, and examples of added procedural burdens that increase capacity demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Task-specific capacity assessment (tailoring capacity to the policy task)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies perform different tasks and each task requires a different type and level of resources; any conceptualization of capacity must be tailored to the specific task (e.g., delivery logistics versus infectious-disease research).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When measuring capacity, compare resources to the particular demands of the policy function under study (use task-relevant indicators rather than cross-agency raw counts). The USPS/CDC vehicle and workforce examples illustrate this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of capacity: funding, nominations, salaries, and resource allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observable indicators of (neglect of) capacity include delegations outpacing appropriations, salaries lagging the private sector, failures to nominate management personnel, and selective presidential investments in agencies tied to agendas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fiscal appropriations, pay-competitiveness, vacancy/nominations data, and White House attention metrics as proxy measures of capacity. The Article references empirical studies documenting these indicators (Bednar & Lewis; Lewis; Verkuil).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural politicking and strategic manipulation of processes
rubrics_metrics.description: When agencies possess high procedural expertise they can manipulate procedures to increase a rule’s chance of survival (expand or limit public participation, manipulate content/language to obscure consequences, time rules to exploit political alignment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This dimension is both a skill/capacity and a behavior to be identified: evaluate tactics used in drafting, consultation, and timing (cites Potter on 'procedural politicking'). It shows that capacity can be used defensively or strategically, not only to increase throughput.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation in capacity across agencies and its effect on presidential control
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity varies greatly within the administrative state; this variation affects theories of presidential control because low-capacity agencies may impede a President’s ability to implement agendas, while high-capacity agencies may be more responsive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rubric implies analysts should model capacity heterogeneity rather than assume uniform high capacity. Empirical measures of capacity are necessary because omitting capacity could bias conclusions about presidential control and policymaking.
